period: Capital in the Middle and New Kingdoms, c. 2050-1070 BC
summary: Homer's 'hundred-gated Thebes', capital of an empire and city of Amun: two of the greatest temples ever built stand in the middle of a modern town.
look: The East Bank is the city of the living. Luxor Temple stands in the centre by the Nile, Karnak lies about 3 km to the north, and the 2.7 km Avenue of Sphinxes joins them. The Luxor Museum and the Mummification Museum are on the Corniche, the riverside road between the two. Across the river, under the Theban hills, is the city of the dead you explored yesterday.
story:
The Egyptians called the city Waset, 'city of the sceptre', or simply Niwt, 'the City'. It was a provincial town until Mentuhotep II, a Theban, reunited Egypt around 2050 BC. Five centuries later Theban princes drove out the Hyksos, and from about 1550 to 1070 BC, the New Kingdom, Thebes was the religious capital of an empire that reached from Sudan to Syria. Its god Amun, merged with the sun as Amun-Ra, became king of the gods, and lived here with his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, the moon. One historian estimates that by 1500 BC Thebes, with perhaps 75,000 people, may have been the largest city in the world.

The Greeks knew of it early. In the Iliad, Achilles speaks of Egyptian Thebes, where treasure is heaped in the houses: 'Thebes of the hundred gates'. The epithet set it apart from seven-gated Thebes in Boeotia. Later Greeks equated Amun with Zeus and called the city Diospolis, City of Zeus.

The glory faded. The Assyrian army of Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 663 BC, and by the first century AD the geographer Strabo found only villages among the ruins. A Roman legion was based inside Luxor Temple, and that camp probably explains the modern name: Arabic al-Uqsur, 'the palaces' or 'the forts', from qasr, a word usually traced back to Latin castrum.

A good rhythm for today: Karnak at opening time, before the heat and the coaches; the air-conditioned Luxor Museum in the middle of the day; Luxor Temple at dusk, when the floodlights come on.
details: From the Corniche, look west over the Nile: the pyramid-shaped peak above the hills is the Qurn, above the Valley of the Kings.
The Avenue of Sphinxes runs straight from Luxor Temple to Karnak: walk a stretch of it in the evening.
Karnak is about 3 km north of Luxor Temple: a short taxi or horse-carriage ride along the Corniche. Agree the fare first.
Luxor Temple is floodlit after dark and stays open into the evening; check today's closing time at the ticket office.
fun_fact: Homer says two hundred men drove out of each of Thebes' hundred gates with horses and chariots. No such city wall has ever been found; one theory is that travellers' tales of temple gateways grew into city gates.
narration:
You are standing in ancient Thebes, which the Egyptians called Waset, the city of the sceptre. For about five hundred years, from roughly 1550 to 1070 BC, this was the religious heart of an empire that reached from Sudan to Syria. Its god was Amun, the hidden one, king of the gods, who lived here with his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, the moon.

The Greeks heard about this place very early. In the Iliad, Achilles talks of Egyptian Thebes, whose houses are stuffed with treasure, Thebes of the hundred gates, where two hundred men ride out of every gate with horses and chariots. The phrase set it apart from seven-gated Thebes in Boeotia, back home in Greece.

Then the glory faded. The Assyrians sacked the city in 663 BC, and later Roman soldiers built a fort inside Luxor Temple. That fort probably gave the town its modern name: al-Uqsur, the castles.

The layout is simple. Luxor Temple stands in the middle of town by the river. Karnak is about 3 kilometres north, joined to it by the Avenue of Sphinxes. The museums sit on the riverside Corniche in between.

A good plan for today: Karnak at opening time, the cool Luxor Museum at midday, and Luxor Temple at dusk when the lights come on. Now look west across the river: that pyramid-shaped peak above the hills watches over the Valley of the Kings, where you were yesterday.

period: New Kingdom, c. 1390-1250 BC, with additions into the Roman period
summary: Not a house for a god but a place where the king's divine spirit was renewed each year; later a Roman fort, a church, and a mosque still in use.
look: You enter from the north through Ramesses II's pylon and walk south along a single axis about 260 metres long. First comes Ramesses' court, with the mosque perched on its east side, then Amenhotep III's tall colonnade, his open sun court and a hall of 32 columns, and finally the dark inner rooms: the Roman chapel, Alexander's shrine, the birth room and the sanctuary. Notice that the axis bends slightly at Ramesses' court.
story:
The Egyptians called it Ipet-resyt, the southern sanctuary, the partner of Karnak at the other end of the avenue. Amenhotep III built the core around 1390-1352 BC. Tutankhamun decorated his great colonnade, and Horemheb put his own name over Tutankhamun's. Ramesses II added the front court, the pylon and the obelisks around 1250 BC, and Alexander the Great rebuilt the sanctuary of the sacred boat.

Most Egyptian temples were houses for a god or for a dead king's cult. This one, according to scholars of the Epigraphic Survey of Chicago House, was the temple of the royal ka, the divine spirit handed from king to king. Each year at the Opet festival Amun came down from Karnak, and in the inner rooms the living king was united with that ka and emerged renewed. The seated colossi at the pylon are ka statues of Ramesses.

The site never really stopped being holy. Around AD 300 the Romans made it the core of a legionary fortress and painted their emperors on its walls. A church followed, and in the 13th century a mosque was built over the rubble of the first court. By then the town lived on top of the temple. When Gaston Maspero began clearing it after 1884, he had to remove houses, stores, huts and pigeon towers standing on an artificial hill some 15 metres high. Excavation continued, on and off, until 1960. The mosque stayed.
details: At the pylon, the two seated colossi are Ramesses II as the royal ka, the very idea this temple celebrated.
On the east side of the first court, the mosque of Abu el-Haggag sits on the ancient columns, at the medieval street level.
The stone is Nubian sandstone from Gebel el-Silsila, between Kom Ombo and Edfu: you drove past the quarries on the 20th.
Come back after dark: the floodlights throw every carving into deep shadow and the reliefs become easy to read.
fun_fact: Alexander the Great had himself shown as pharaoh in the heart of this temple, and later tradition had him crowned here. He may never have travelled further south than Memphis.
narration:
This is Luxor Temple, which the Egyptians called Ipet resyt, the southern sanctuary. It is laid out like a corridor, about 260 metres long, and you will walk it from north to south.

Amenhotep the Third built the heart of it, more than 3,300 years ago. Tutankhamun decorated his great colonnade. Ramesses the Second added the front court, the gateway and the obelisks. Alexander the Great rebuilt the inner shrine.

Here is the surprising part. Most temples were houses for a god. This one, according to the scholars who study it, was a temple of the royal ka, the divine spirit that passed from one king to the next. Once a year, at the Opet festival, Amun came down from Karnak, and in the dark rooms at the back the living king was united with that spirit and came out renewed.

And it never stopped being holy. Roman soldiers turned it into a fortress and painted their emperors inside. In the 13th century a mosque rose on the rubble, and it is still in use. When the French scholar Gaston Maspero began clearing the site in the 1880s, the temple lay under a hill of houses and pigeon towers about 15 metres high.

Come back after dark, when the lights pick out every carving. For now, look at the two seated giants at the gate: they are Ramesses as that royal spirit, welcoming you in.

period: New Kingdom to 30th Dynasty; sphinxes of Nectanebo I, 380-362 BC
summary: A 2.7 km sacred road lined with 1,057 statues, buried under the town for centuries and reopened with a pharaonic parade in November 2021.
look: In front of Luxor Temple the avenue runs north from the pylon, lined on both sides with human-headed sphinxes on low pedestals, each facing its twin across the road. It continues dead straight for 2.7 km to Karnak; near the Karnak end the sphinxes have rams' heads. Long stretches are open to walk, and it is at its best in the evening light.
story:
The Egyptians called it the 'path of god'. Building began in the New Kingdom, but the sphinxes nearest Luxor Temple are later: Nectanebo I, of the last native dynasty (380-362 BC), lined the road with human-headed sphinxes, probably replacing older ones. Nearer Karnak the shapes change: ram-headed lions set up under Tutankhamun between Karnak and the temple of Mut, and full rams of Amenhotep III brought from elsewhere. The count today is 1,057 statues: 807 sphinxes and 250 with rams' heads.

This was the land route of the Opet festival. Six way stations let the priests set down Amun's boat-shrine and rest; one of them, by its name, 'cooled the oar of Amun'. A small mudbrick shrine to Serapis and Isis, built in AD 126 in the courtyard of Nectanebo I and presented to the emperor Hadrian on his birthday, shows the road was still used in Roman times.

Then the town swallowed it. In 1893 Georges Daressy reported that at Luxor it lay below the groundwater and could not be dug. The first sphinxes came back in 1949, when the Egyptian archaeologist Mohammed Zakaria Ghoneim found eight near the temple. The full route was traced between 1984 and 2000, and clearing it meant demolishing whole streets of houses. Excavators also reported Roman-era workshops along the way, including what they took to be wine presses.

On 25 November 2021 the avenue reopened with a televised parade: performers in pharaonic dress, an orchestra, horse-drawn carriages and three golden barques for Amun, Mut and Khonsu.
details: Each sphinx faces its twin across the road: walk down the middle, as the god's boat once did.
Look at the faces: some are ancient and weathered, others pieced together from fragments by restorers.
Look for the hieroglyphs on the sphinx bases near Luxor Temple, the dedication of Nectanebo I.
Near Karnak the heads become rams, Amun's sacred animal: you will meet more at Karnak's entrance.
fun_fact: Napoleon's scholars, in the Description de l'Egypte of 1809, guessed the avenue had over 600 sphinxes. Seventy years of digging have raised the count to 1,057.
narration:
You are on the Avenue of Sphinxes, the sacred road the Egyptians called the path of god. It runs dead straight for 2.7 kilometres from Luxor Temple to Karnak, and more than a thousand statues lined it.

The human-headed sphinxes nearest Luxor Temple were set up by Nectanebo the First, one of the last native Egyptian pharaohs, around 380 BC. Nearer Karnak, the heads turn into rams, the sacred animal of Amun. The count today is 1,057 statues.

This was the land route of the Opet festival. Once a year priests carried Amun's statue in a gilded boat on their shoulders from Karnak to Luxor, stopping at six resting stations along the way. One of them, by its name, cooled the oar of Amun.

Then the town grew over it. By the 19th century most of the road lay buried under houses, below the water table. The first sphinxes came back in 1949, and the dig went on, on and off, for seventy years, clearing whole streets of houses. In November 2021 the full avenue reopened with a parade straight out of a film: performers in pharaonic costume, an orchestra, and three golden boats for Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu.

Walk a stretch of it now, ideally at dusk. Look at the faces of the sphinxes. Some are ancient and weathered, some patched together by restorers, and each one stares across the road at its twin.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1250 BC
summary: One obelisk is still here. Its twin has stood in Paris since 1836, and France's thank-you was a clock that has hardly ever worked.
look: Facing the temple from the avenue, the pylon rises ahead of you, its two towers carved with Ramesses II's battle of Kadesh. Two seated colossi of the king flank the gateway, with standing statues of him further out. The surviving obelisk of red Aswan granite stands on the left; its twin stood on the right until 1831.
story:
Ramesses II added this gateway about 150 years after Amenhotep III built the temple. The towers are a giant billboard for the battle of Kadesh, fought in Syria in May 1274 BC against the Hittite king Muwatalli II: on one side the Egyptian camp and the king in council with his officers, on the other the king charging in his chariot as the enemy is driven into the river Orontes. Hittite records say Ramesses withdrew; he carved a triumph anyway, at Luxor and in several other temples.

In front stood a pair of obelisks of slightly different heights. The shorter one sat on a taller base and further forward, so that from the avenue they looked equal. In November 1830 Muhammad Ali, ruler of Egypt, gave both to France, urged on by Champollion. The western one was lowered in 1831, sailed to France on a ship built for the job and named the Luxor, and raised in the Place de la Concorde in 1836, 23 metres tall. Champollion died in 1832 and never saw it there. By the usual story France's return gift, in the 1840s, was the clock now on the Citadel in Cairo, which has rarely worked. The move cost about 2.5 million francs, which probably saved the second obelisk; France formally renounced it in 1981.

The bases carried baboons raising their arms to the rising sun, carved with frank anatomical detail. Part of the original base went to Paris too, was judged too indecent for a public square, and ended up in the Louvre.
details: On the base of the remaining obelisk, find the baboons raising their paws to greet the rising sun.
In low sun, look on the pylon towers for the Kadesh scenes: the camp, the council of war and the king's chariot charge.
Line the obelisk up against the edge of the pylon: it leans slightly.
Look at the space on the right of the gate where the Paris obelisk stood, and imagine the matching pair.
fun_fact: Muhammad Ali had first promised the Luxor obelisks to Britain. On French advice he offered the British Hatshepsut's obelisk at Karnak instead, which Champollion knew was nearly impossible to extract. It is still standing there.
narration:
In front of you is the main gate of Luxor Temple, the pylon of Ramesses the Second, with one lonely obelisk on the left.

There used to be two. They were cut from red granite at Aswan and were slightly different heights, so the builders put the shorter one on a taller base and set it further forward. From the avenue, the pair looked identical. In 1830 Muhammad Ali, the ruler of Egypt, gave both to France. The one on the right was lowered, sailed to France on a ship named Luxor, and since 1836 it has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris. In return, so the story goes, France sent a clock, which went to the Citadel in Cairo and has hardly ever worked. Moving it cost so much that the second never left.

Now look at the pylon towers. Ramesses filled them with the battle of Kadesh, fought against the Hittites in Syria in 1274 BC. On one side the Egyptian camp and the king in council, on the other the king charging in his chariot while his enemies tumble into the river. In truth the battle was a draw at best, but Ramesses carved it as a triumph, here and in several other temples.

Finally, look at the base of the obelisk. Those carved baboons are raising their arms to greet the rising sun. Part of the matching base went to Paris too, but the baboons were judged too rude for a public square, and they ended up in the Louvre.

period: Ayyubid, 13th century, built over a temple of c. 1250 BC
summary: A working mosque perched on the pharaoh's columns, its old door opening onto thin air: it was built when the temple lay buried under the town.
look: Look up at the east side of the court of Ramesses II: the mosque sits on top of the ancient walls and columns, at the level of the medieval town. Its old door hangs high above the courtyard floor, and Ramesside columns stand half embedded in its walls. The two mud-brick minarets are its oldest parts; today's entrance is from the street outside the temple.
story:
Yusuf Abu el-Haggag was a Sufi holy man, by tradition from Baghdad, who settled in Luxor and became its patron saint. The mosque over his tomb was built in the 13th century, in the Ayyubid period under Sultan al-Salih Ayyub, on the site of a demolished church. By then the temple had vanished under centuries of mud-brick houses and rubbish, and the builders worked on top of the mound, using whatever ancient walls and columns still showed.

When archaeologists dug the temple out from the 1880s, they cleared the village but left the mosque. So now it floats: its floor is at medieval street level, high above the court, and the old door opens onto air. With the church before it, the site has been a place of worship, under different gods, for well over 3,000 years.

After a fire in June 2007 the mosque was restored over two years from 2009, and the work exposed columns and lintels inscribed under Ramesses II inside the building.

Every year, about two weeks before Ramadan, Luxor celebrates the saint's mawlid. For three days there are horse races, Sufi music and stick fighting, and his descendants carry boats in procession around the temple, said to recall his journey to Egypt. Many people, including the organisers, see an echo of the Opet festival, when the boats of the gods passed through the same streets.
details: East side of the first court: the mosque's old door, hanging high in the wall above the ancient floor.
Spot the Ramesside papyrus-bud columns half swallowed by the mosque's walls.
The older minaret, mud brick with a square lower storey and two round ones above, is the mosque's oldest part.
To visit the mosque itself, enter from the street side outside prayer times, with shoulders and knees covered.
fun_fact: The mosque's old doorway leads nowhere: step through it from inside and you would drop straight into Ramesses II's courtyard.
narration:
Look up at the east side of this courtyard. That building sitting on top of the pharaoh's columns is a working mosque, the mosque of Abu el-Haggag, and it has been here since the 13th century.

When it was built, the temple had disappeared. Centuries of mud brick houses and rubbish had raised the ground by many metres, and the builders simply put the mosque on top, over the remains of an older church, using whatever ancient stone stuck out.

In the 1880s archaeologists began digging the temple out. They cleared away the village, but they left the mosque. So now it floats. Its floor is at medieval street level, and its old door opens onto thin air, high above the court of Ramesses.

The saint buried inside, Yusuf Abu el-Haggag, was a Sufi holy man said to have come from Baghdad. He is still the patron of Luxor. Every year, shortly before Ramadan, the town holds his festival: three days of music, horse races and stick fighting, with boats carried in procession around the temple. Many people here see in it an echo of the ancient Opet festival, when the boats of the gods passed this way.

So this spot has been holy for more than 3,000 years: temple, church, mosque. Now find the old doorway in the mosque wall, hanging above your head with nowhere to go.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1250 BC; triple shrine c. 1470 BC
summary: Ramesses II squeezed a whole court in front of an older temple, bent it to fit, and kept a shrine of Hatshepsut's time in the corner.
look: Through the pylon you enter a court ringed by a double row of papyrus-bud columns, 74 in all, with standing colossi of the king between the columns on the far side. In the corner to your right as you enter is the small triple shrine for the sacred boats. Stand in the middle and you will see the axis bend: the court is angled away from the rest of the temple.
story:
Ramesses II added this court about 150 years after Amenhotep III built the temple, and it does not sit straight. The usual explanation is that the builders had to respect an older shrine already standing here and line the new gate up with the road from Karnak.

That shrine, in the north-west corner, is older than anything around it: a way station with three chapels for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu, built under Hatshepsut and Thutmose III and reused by Ramesses.

The walls are a Ramesside family album. On the western side a procession of the king's sons leads fattened bulls with decorated horns towards a carving of this very temple as it looked on opening day: the pylon with its flagpoles, the colossi and both obelisks, including the one now in Paris.

Among the colossi, look at the king's legs. A small queen stands there, reaching only to his knee: Nefertari, his great royal wife, whose tomb is the finest in the Valley of the Queens.
details: Right as you enter: the triple shrine of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III, with chapels for Amun, Mut and Khonsu.
On the western walls, find Ramesses' sons leading fattened bulls towards a carving of the pylon with flags and obelisks.
At the feet of the standing colossi, look for Queen Nefertari, carved knee-high against the king's leg.
Look up at the east colonnade: the mosque of Abu el-Haggag sits right on top of the ancient columns.
fun_fact: Ramesses' carvers drew this temple on its own wall, flags flying and both obelisks in place: a 3,200-year-old picture of the Paris obelisk at home.
narration:
You are now inside the court of Ramesses the Second, surrounded by a double row of stone papyrus stalks, 74 columns in all. Between the columns on the far side stand colossal statues of the king.

Ramesses built this court about 150 years after the rest of the temple, and he had a problem. In the corner on your right stood an older shrine, built under Hatshepsut and Thutmose the Third, a resting place for the sacred boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu. He kept it, and built around it. Notice too that the whole court sits at a slight angle to the temple beyond, probably to line it up with the road from Karnak.

The walls are a family album. On the western side, a line of the king's sons leads fattened bulls with decorated horns towards a picture of this very temple: the pylon with its flagpoles, the colossi and both obelisks, including the one now in Paris.

Now walk to one of the standing colossi and look down by the king's leg. That small woman, reaching only to his knee, is Queen Nefertari, his great royal wife.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III to Tutankhamun, c. 1360-1323 BC
summary: Fourteen giant stone papyrus stalks, and on the walls the best picture of an ancient Egyptian festival: boats, drums, acrobats and plenty of beer.
look: You walk down a corridor of fourteen huge papyrus columns with open, flower-shaped capitals, in two rows of seven. The side walls, only partly standing, carry the Opet procession in long bands of relief: the west wall, on your right as you walk south, shows the journey from Karnak to Luxor, and the east wall the journey back. Low morning or evening light makes the carving easiest to read.
story:
Amenhotep III built this as the grand entrance to his temple. Some Egyptologists think it was meant to be the central aisle of a much larger hall that was never finished. It became the model for the giant central aisle of the Hypostyle Hall at Karnak.

He died before the walls were carved. The decoration was done under Tutankhamun, after the Amarna years, as a loud statement that the old gods and their festivals were back. Horemheb later put his own name over Tutankhamun's.

The subject is the Opet festival, held in the second month of the flood season. Amun, Mut and Khonsu left Karnak in their gilded boat-shrines, were towed upriver to Luxor, stayed while the king renewed his divine ka, and went home again. Under Thutmose III the festival lasted 11 days; by the end of Ramesses III's reign, 27.

The walls catch the crowd: soldiers and charioteers, Nubian drummers, women shaking sistra, acrobats bending over backwards, butchers at work for the feast, and offering tables piled with bread and jars of beer. It is a rare view of an Egyptian party rather than a funeral. The Epigraphic Survey of Chicago House recorded every surviving line, and its published drawings show detail that the eroded stone now hides.
details: West wall, on your right walking south: the boats sail from Karnak to Luxor, towed by men on the bank.
Along the walls, look for the acrobats bending backwards and the Nubian drummers in the marching crowd.
East wall, on your left: the return journey to Karnak.
Look up at the open papyrus capitals: Karnak's tallest columns copy this design.
Many royal names here are Horemheb's, cut over Tutankhamun's.
fun_fact: The festival kept growing: 11 days under Thutmose III, 24 at the start of Ramesses III's reign and 27 by its end. Nearly a month of holiday with free bread and beer.
narration:
You are walking down the processional colonnade of Amenhotep the Third: fourteen giant columns shaped like papyrus stalks, their tops opening like flowers. Some Egyptologists think it was meant to be the central aisle of a far bigger hall that was never finished. Either way, it became the model for the great hall at Karnak.

The king died before the walls were carved, and the job fell to the young Tutankhamun. After Akhenaten's revolution, he used these walls to announce that the old gods and their festivals were back. Later, Horemheb put his own name over Tutankhamun's.

The subject is the Opet festival. Each year, in the flood season, Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu left Karnak in gilded boat shrines and were towed upriver to this temple, where the king renewed his divine spirit. Under Thutmose the Third the festival lasted 11 days. Under Ramesses the Third, 27.

On the wall to your right as you walk south, the boats leave Karnak and travel here. On the left wall, they go home. Around them is the crowd: soldiers, charioteers, Nubian drummers, women shaking rattles, butchers preparing the feast, and tables loaded with bread and beer. This is ancient Egypt having a party.

Walk slowly along the walls and look for the acrobats, bending so far backwards that their hands touch the ground behind them.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: The most elegant court in Egypt kept a secret: in 1989 workers found 26 superb statues buried beneath its floor.
look: Beyond the colonnade opens a wide court framed on three sides by double rows of columns, each carved as a bundle of papyrus stems. At the far, southern end, a denser forest of 32 columns forms the hall that leads into the inner rooms. The 1989 cachette was found under the floor of this court.
story:
Amenhotep III built this sun court, open to the sky, as the forecourt of his temple. Its bundled papyrus columns are among the finest work of the 18th Dynasty, before the Ramesside builders went for sheer size.

In 1989 workers checking the foundations of the court hit a pit packed with statues, 26 of them, most in near-perfect condition. They had been buried on purpose in antiquity, most accounts say in the Roman period. A statue dedicated to a god could not simply be thrown away; when the temple needed the space, priests gave the statues a sacred burial instead.

The star is a red quartzite Amenhotep III, 2.49 metres tall, standing on a sledge as if he were a cult image about to be dragged in procession. Others include Horemheb kneeling before the god Atum, and the goddesses Hathor and Iunyt. All are now in the Luxor Museum, in a hall built for them, and you can see them later today.
details: Look at the column shafts: each is carved as a bundle of papyrus stems bound together, with a closed bud on top.
Stand in the middle of the court and look back north: the colonnade frames the view towards the pylon.
At the south end, enter the hall of 32 columns, the last roofed space before the inner rooms.
Come back after dark: floodlit, the double rows of columns throw long shadows across the court.
fun_fact: For a century after the excavation, millions of visitors crossed this court without knowing that 26 statues lay under their feet.
narration:
This open court is the sun court of Amenhotep the Third, who ruled from about 1390 to 1352 BC. Look at the columns in their double rows: each one is carved as a bundle of papyrus stems tied together, with a closed bud on top.

In 1989, workers checking the foundations of this court found a pit full of statues. Twenty six of them, almost perfect. Priests had buried them on purpose in ancient times, probably in the Roman period. A statue given to a god could not be thrown away, so when it was no longer wanted, it got a sacred burial instead.

The finest is Amenhotep the Third himself, in red quartzite, about 2 and a half metres tall, standing on a sledge as if waiting to be pulled along in a procession. With him came Horemheb kneeling before the god Atum, and statues of goddesses. They are all in the Luxor Museum now, in a hall built specially for them.

For a century, millions of visitors walked over that treasure without knowing. Now look south: the forest of 32 columns ahead leads into the dark inner rooms.

summary: Around AD 300 Roman soldiers turned a pharaoh's hall into a shrine of the emperors, plastered over the gods and painted four rulers in purple.
look: Just south of the 32-column hall is a room whose doorway at the back was blocked and turned into a curved niche, an apse, framed by columns. Patches of plaster with Roman paintings cover the walls: soldiers, horses and officials, and in the apse the faded figures of the four emperors. Where the plaster has fallen, Amenhotep III's carved gods show through underneath.
story:
Around AD 300 the emperor Diocletian reorganised the defence of Egypt's southern frontier and turned Luxor Temple into the heart of a fortified camp for a legion. The fort's walls ran round the temple, and traces of its gates and streets survive outside.

Inside, the Romans chose a room of Amenhotep III's temple, once associated with the goddess Mut, and made it the shrine of the imperial cult. They blocked the doorway to the inner temple and turned it into an apse, covered the hieroglyphs with plaster and painted everything afresh. In the apse stood the four rulers of the Tetrarchy, Diocletian's system for governing the empire: two senior emperors, Diocletian and Maximian, and two juniors, Galerius and Constantius, in imperial purple. Along the side walls officials and soldiers with horses approach them. Here the legion honoured its emperors, and its standards were probably kept here. Later the room served as a church.

For centuries the paintings sat under grime and soot, and some details survive only in 19th-century copies by travellers. Between 2005 and 2008 conservators working for the American Research Center in Egypt cleaned them, and faces and colours came back. Painted shrines of the emperors are very rare survivals anywhere in the Roman world.
details: In the apse at the back, look for the faded figures of the four emperors in purple.
On the side walls, find the Roman procession: soldiers, horses and officials in late Roman dress.
Where the plaster has fallen, Amenhotep III and Amun show through, carved in relief beneath the Roman paint.
Outside the temple, look for the remains of the Roman fortress walls and gates.
fun_fact: One of the four emperors painted here is Galerius, whose triumphal arch and Rotunda still stand in Thessaloniki.
narration:
This room is a surprise: a Roman chapel inside a pharaoh's temple. Around AD 300, the emperor Diocletian turned Luxor Temple into the heart of a fortress for a Roman legion, and this hall, built by Amenhotep the Third, became a shrine to the emperors.

The Romans blocked the doorway at the back and turned it into a curved niche. Then they plastered over the ancient gods and painted everything again in their own style. In the niche stood the four rulers of the empire at that time, the Tetrarchs: two senior emperors, Diocletian and Maximian, and two juniors, Constantius and Galerius, all in imperial purple. Along the side walls, officials, soldiers and horses walk towards them in procession. This is where the legion honoured its emperors as near gods.

One of those four men has a link to home. Galerius built the triumphal arch and the Rotunda that still stand in Thessaloniki.

For centuries the paintings sat under dirt and soot. Between 2005 and 2008, conservators from the American Research Center in Egypt cleaned them, and faces and colours came back. Very few painted shrines of the emperors survive anywhere in the Roman world.

Now look where the plaster has fallen away. Underneath the Roman soldiers, Amenhotep's carved gods are still there, peeking out after 1,700 years.

period: Macedonian, Alexander the Great, c. 330 BC; birth room of Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: A Macedonian dressed as pharaoh: Alexander rebuilt the shrine of Amun's boat, and next door Amenhotep III's carved birth story makes him the god's son.
look: In the middle of a room, once a hall of four columns, stands a free-standing stone shrine open at both ends, where Amun's boat rested during the Opet festival. Its outer walls show Alexander as pharaoh, in Egyptian crowns, offering to Amun. The birth room is the chamber to the east, on your left as you face south, and the innermost sanctuary lies beyond, at the very end of the axis.
story:
Alexander reached Egypt late in 332 BC and was welcomed as the man who ended Persian rule. Early in 331 BC he crossed the desert to the oracle of Amun at Siwa, which you visited on the 14th, and came away hailed as the son of Zeus-Ammon. Amun of Thebes was the same god, so honouring him here made perfect sense.

In Alexander's name the four columns of Amenhotep III's barque room were removed and this shrine built inside it. On its walls Alexander, with a pharaoh's names in cartouches, offers to Amun, including Amun in the form of Min, the fertility god, ithyphallic and unembarrassed. Tradition had Alexander crowned at Luxor; in fact he may never have travelled south of Memphis. The carving was done by Egyptian priests and sculptors who knew the old rules exactly.

The birth room tells an older version of the same claim. Amenhotep III's mother, Queen Mutemwiya, is visited by Amun, who has taken the form of her husband Thutmose IV. The ram-headed potter god Khnum shapes the baby and his ka on a wheel, and goddesses attend the birth and the nursing. The cycle copies Hatshepsut's divine birth at Deir el-Bahari, which you saw on the 21st.

Beyond lies the sanctuary where Amun's statue stood, the end of a line some 260 metres from the pylon.
details: On the shrine's outer walls, find Alexander in pharaoh's crown, offering to Amun.
Look for Amun-Min, one arm raised with a flail behind it, unmistakably male.
Find Alexander's cartouche: the hieroglyphs spell out his Greek name.
In the birth room to the east, find Khnum at his potter's wheel shaping the baby king and his double.
Walk to the end of the axis and look back north towards the pylon, about 260 metres away.
fun_fact: In his cartouches Alexander carries a full pharaoh's throne name, Setepenre Meryamun, 'chosen of Ra, beloved of Amun', followed by Alexandros spelled out in hieroglyphs.
narration:
You are at the heart of the temple. The stone shrine in front of you, open at both ends, is where the sacred boat of Amun rested during the Opet festival. And the pharaoh on its walls, offering to the god, is Alexander the Great.

Alexander reached Egypt in 332 BC and was welcomed as the man who ended Persian rule. You saw on the 14th where he went next: across the desert to the oracle of Amun at Siwa, where he was hailed as the son of Zeus Ammon. Amun of Thebes was the same god, so in Alexander's name the old shrine of Amenhotep the Third was cleared out and this one built inside it. Egyptian sculptors carved him exactly like a pharaoh, with crowns and cartouches. One of the gods he offers to is Amun in the form of Min, the fertility god, very obviously male. The funny thing is that Alexander may never have come this far south at all.

Through the doorway to the east is the birth room, where Amenhotep the Third told his own divine origin story. The god Amun visits his mother, Queen Mutemwiya, disguised as her husband. The ram-headed potter god Khnum shapes the baby on his wheel. It is the same story Hatshepsut carved at Deir el-Bahari, which you saw on the 21st.

Now look for Alexander's cartouche on the shrine wall. Those hieroglyphs spell out his Greek name, Alexandros.

period: Middle Kingdom to Ptolemaic, c. 1950-30 BC
summary: Two thousand years of kings adding gates, halls and obelisks to one god's house: less a temple than a city of temples.
look: You visit the Precinct of Amun-Ra, about 25 hectares inside mud-brick walls. The main axis runs east from the old quay: avenue of rams, first pylon, Great Court, Hypostyle Hall, obelisks, sanctuary and Thutmose III's festival hall at the far end. A second axis runs south through more pylons towards the Precinct of Mut, and the Sacred Lake lies in the angle between the two.
story:
The Egyptians called it Ipet-isut, usually translated 'the most select of places'; the name Karnak comes from the modern village nearby. Building began under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom, around 1950 BC, and went on into Ptolemaic times: nearly 2,000 years and some 30 pharaohs. Every king who could afford it added a gate, a hall, an obelisk or a chapel, or at least carved his name over someone else's. Most of what stands is New Kingdom.

Karnak has four parts: the Precinct of Amun-Ra, which you visit; the Precinct of Mut, his wife, to the south; the Precinct of Montu, the old war god of Thebes, to the north; and to the east the site of Akhenaten's temple to the Aten, demolished soon after his death. Their son Khonsu, the moon, has his own temple inside Amun's enclosure.

It was the richest institution in Egypt. The Great Harris Papyrus says Ramesses III gave the temples of Amun 86,486 people and vast estates.

The emperor Constantius II ordered pagan temples closed in AD 356, and Christians later built churches among the ruins. The first European description dates from 1589.

A plan: come at opening and allow at least three hours. Walk the main axis first, then turn south to the Sacred Lake and the scarab, and finish at the Temple of Khonsu and the Open Air Museum.
details: Count the pylons as you go: six on the main east-west axis, four more on the southern axis.
The Open Air Museum, north of the Great Court, needs a separate ticket: ask at the ticket office when you arrive.
Bring water and a hat: there is little shade except in the Hypostyle Hall.
The tiered stands by the Sacred Lake are for the evening sound and light show.
fun_fact: According to the Great Harris Papyrus, Ramesses III gave the temples of Amun 86,486 people, along with fields, herds and ships.
narration:
Welcome to Karnak, which the Egyptians called Ipet isut, the most select of places. This was the house of Amun, king of the gods, and for almost 2,000 years, from about 1950 BC into the age of the Ptolemies, some 30 pharaohs kept adding to it. Every ruler who could afford it built a gate, a hall, an obelisk or a chapel, or at least carved his name over someone else's. The result is less a temple than a city of temples.

What you are visiting is the precinct of Amun Ra, about 25 hectares inside mud brick walls. Next door, to the south, is the precinct of his wife Mut, and to the north that of Montu, the old war god of Thebes. Their son Khonsu, the moon, has his own temple inside this enclosure.

Karnak was also the richest institution in the land. One papyrus records that Ramesses the Third gave the temples of Amun more than 86,000 people and huge estates.

The plan has two axes. The main one runs east from the old riverside quay: rams, first pylon, great court, the forest of columns, obelisks, sanctuary, and the festival hall at the far end. A second runs south towards Mut's temple. Allow at least three hours, and walk the main axis first, while it is still cool.

Now look straight ahead at the first pylon. It is the youngest building on this axis, and it was never finished.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1250 BC; quay texts c. 900-650 BC
summary: Amun's rams guard the entrance, each sheltering a little statue of the king between its paws, where the god's boat once came ashore.
look: From the entrance plaza you walk east along a short avenue of criosphinxes, lion bodies with rams' heads, lying on pedestals on both sides of the path. Behind you, towards the river, is the raised platform of the ancient quay; ahead rises the first pylon. Look between the front paws of each ram for a small standing figure of the king.
story:
The ram was Amun's sacred animal, so at his temple the sphinxes have rams' heads on lions' bodies. Each one shelters a small statue of the king between its front paws: the god protecting the pharaoh. Most were made under Ramesses II. When the Great Court was later built over the avenue, the rams in its way were moved and lined up along its sides, where you will see them in a moment.

In front of them is the quay, a stone platform that once looked onto a canal linked to the Nile. Here Amun's boat-shrine was carried down to the water at the start of his journeys: south to Luxor Temple for the Opet festival, or across the river to the West Bank for the Beautiful Festival of the Valley.

On the face of the quay, priests of the Third Intermediate Period carved the height reached by the Nile flood in particular years. For historians these short notes are precious: they help date the reigns of the period and track the behaviour of the river.

Close to the quay stands a small way station for the sacred boat, built by Hakoris, a king of the 29th Dynasty in the early 4th century BC, one of the last native pharaohs.
details: Between the paws of each ram, find the small figure of the king standing under the god's chin.
Look at the horns: Amun's ram has horns curling down round the ears, not Khnum's long wavy ones.
Behind you, towards the river: the stone platform of the ancient quay, with flood-level notes carved on its face.
Ahead, the first pylon: notice the bare, undecorated stone of an unfinished gate.
fun_fact: Amun's ram has horns that curl round its ears. Khnum's ram, which you saw at Esna and Elephantine, has long wavy horns sticking out sideways, from an older breed of sheep that later disappeared.
narration:
You are walking between Amun's rams. The ram was the sacred animal of Amun, so at his temple the sphinxes have lion bodies and rams' heads. Look between the front paws of any of them: each one shelters a small statue of the king, standing safe under the god's chin. Most were set up by Ramesses the Second.

Notice the horns. Amun's ram has horns that curl down around its ears. The ram of Khnum, the potter god you met at Esna and Aswan, has long wavy horns sticking out sideways, from an older breed of sheep. Egyptians could tell their gods apart by their sheep.

Now turn round and look back towards the river. That raised stone platform was the ancient quay. A canal joined it to the Nile, and here the priests carried Amun's gilded boat down to the water at the start of his great festivals: south to Luxor Temple for Opet, or across the river to the West Bank. On the face of the quay, priests of the centuries after 900 BC carved the height the Nile flood reached in particular years. To historians these notes are gold: they help date the kings and track the river.

Nearby is a small shrine where the sacred boat could rest, built by Hakoris, one of the last native kings, in the 4th century BC.

Then turn east again. Ahead of you rises the first pylon, 113 metres wide. Look at its surface: almost completely bare. It was never finished.
